title: Wealth Taxes Could Kill Privately-Owned Companies
gist: Argues California's Proposition 40 (one-time up-to-5% billionaire wealth tax) taxes not money but control: illiquid founder stakes must be sold at forced-seller discounts, and even one outside shareholder imposes fiduciary shareholder-value duties (eBay v. Newmark), turning mission-driven private firms like In-N-Out into diffusely held corporations. Prop 40's rule valuing control stakes by voting power will force founders to lose control, raising a Takings Clause question that also bears on Ro Khanna's proposed 2% federal tax over $50M.

insights.claim: California's Proposition 40, on the November ballot, would impose a one-time tax of up to five percent on the wealth of the state's billionaire residents.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: A one-time 5% levy on illiquid founder stakes could force sizable secondary supply of private-company shares.
insights.quote: This November, California will vote on Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax of up to five percent on the wealth of the state’s billionaire residents.

insights.claim: In-N-Out owner Lynsi Snyder announced a move of her family to Tennessee and a second In-N-Out headquarters there, three months before the initiative that became Proposition 40 was filed.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Billionaire relocation from California is already underway ahead of wealth-tax votes, shifting HQs and tax base to states like Tennessee.
insights.quote: Three months later, the initiative that would become Proposition 40 was filed with the California Attorney General.

insights.claim: The mainstream Prop 40 debate (revenue estimates, business formation, billionaire flight) wrongly shares the assumption that what is being taxed is just money, ignoring the governance rights embedded in ownership.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Market models of wealth-tax impact that treat it as a pure cash drain miss control-loss and forced-restructuring effects.
insights.quote: All of these debates share the single assumption that what’s being taxed is just money.

insights.claim: Proposition 40's valuation rules presume a taxpayer's ownership share is at least their share of voting/control rights, meaning controlling stakes are valued as voting percentage times the value of all shares rather than by economic ownership.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Dual-class founders (super-voting shares) face liabilities far exceeding their economic stake, sharply raising forced-sale and relocation incentives.
insights.quote: For any interests that confer voting or other direct control rights, the percentage of the business entity owned by the taxpayer shall be presumed to be not less than the taxpayer’s percentage
insights.locator: They will not have to consider

insights.claim: Because Prop 40 values control shares by voting power rather than standard appraisal practice, the author predicts many California founders will be forced to surrender control of their companies entirely.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Expect founder-controlled California companies to pre-emptively relocate, restructure dual-class setups, or sell control blocks.
insights.quote: Foreseeably, this will force many California founders to surrender control of their companies entirely.

insights.claim: Congressman Ro Khanna has endorsed a federal wealth tax with a 2% annual levy on all wealth over $50 million, a threshold that reaches far beyond billionaires to founders and family businesses.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: A federal version removes the interstate-relocation escape valve and would hit a vastly larger universe of private-company owners annually.
insights.quote: Congressman Ro Khanna recently endorsed a federal version of the wealth tax, which contains a 2% annual tax on all wealth over $50 million.

insights.claim: A small preferred-share round that values a private company at $10 billion does not mean a founder's 50% common stake can actually be sold for $5 billion; the headline valuation is an inference from a structurally different security.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Wealth taxes anchored to last-round marks overstate liquidation value of founder common stock, creating outsized real tax burdens.
insights.quote: a price established by a small transaction does not predict the price at which a large block of shares can be sold.

insights.claim: A founder forced to raise $250 million in cash from private shares faces months-long processes, rights of first refusal, board approvals, buyer demands for board seats, possible regulatory approval, and counterparties who all know she is a forced seller.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Forced-seller dynamics create discounted block sales — an opportunity for secondary buyers and a hit to founders.
insights.quote: Throughout all of this, every person sitting across the table knows the same thing: she has to sell.

insights.claim: Because block sales clear below headline valuations, a founder must liquidate more shares than the nominal tax rate implies, which can push a just-over-50% holder below control.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Even a 5% tax can trigger change of control for founders near the 50% threshold.
insights.quote: To meet her tax liability, Alice has to liquidate more shares than the headline valuation would suggest.

insights.claim: When a company has never sold shares or raised outside capital, as with In-N-Out over 75 years, there are no reference transactions at all, so the state must invent a valuation.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Valuation disputes over closely held firms will be a major litigation and advisory battleground under any wealth tax.
insights.quote: Nobody knows what In-N-Out Burger is worth.

insights.claim: Wealth taxes treat billionaire wealth as deferred consumption, but founders accumulate wealth to direct resources toward a mission, so taxing it redistributes control, not just consumption.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Policy that forces founders to dilute shifts corporate strategy toward diffuse-shareholder norms.
insights.quote: A founder accumulates wealth precisely because he or she does not want to consume the underlying resources. They want to direct them

insights.claim: A founder's control can itself be part of what makes the company valuable, so the company with and without founder control are not the same asset; the tax capitalizes the value of authority and then forces its dilution.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Forced dilution may destroy part of the very value being taxed, lowering the realized base.
insights.quote: Acme under Alice’s direct control and Acme without it are not really the same asset.

insights.claim: In-N-Out can refuse to franchise, keep a roughly four-item menu, and pay associates/managers far above competitors only because it answers to a single owner, Lynsi Snyder.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Sole-owner private firms can sustain non-profit-maximizing strategies that public or diffusely held firms cannot.
insights.quote: In-N-Out can do all of this for one reason: because it answers to exactly one person, Lynsi Snyder

insights.claim: For a sole-owned company, sovereignty over the business is lost with the very first outside investor, well before the 50% control threshold is breached, because fiduciary duties to minority holders kick in.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Even small forced sales fundamentally change governance of family-controlled firms, not just their cap tables.
insights.quote: Even though her control is lost at 50%, her sovereignty over the business is lost with the first outside investor.
insights.locator: If she had stayed in California

insights.claim: Lynsi Snyder has said In-N-Out is 'not about the money' and she would never sell barring divine intervention, illustrating mission-driven ownership a wealth tax would force into shareholder-value framing.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Owners of iconic private brands are motivated to relocate rather than accept forced outside ownership.
insights.quote: Unless God sends a lightning bolt down and changes my heart miraculously, I would not ever sell.

insights.claim: A wealth tax progressively converts institutions governed by a particular private purpose into ones governed by the logic of shareholder maximalism.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Expect more monetization and profit-maximization pressure at formerly mission-driven private firms over time.
insights.quote: A wealth tax progressively converts an institution governed according to a particular private telos into one governed by the logic of shareholder maximalism.

insights.claim: Ironically, a wealth tax forces onto every private institution the commodification that critics have long blamed on capitalism, via forced liquidation into shareholder capitalism.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Wealth taxes may accelerate financialization of private firms rather than counter it.
insights.quote: In practice, a wealth tax forces this onto every private institution via forced liquidation and transformation into an engine of shareholder capitalism.
insights.locator: This is what makes the wealth

insights.claim: In eBay v. Newmark, the Delaware Court of Chancery rejected Craigslist founders' attempt to preserve a non-monetizing culture via a rights plan, because eBay held a minority stake.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Delaware law means any outside shareholder can constrain founder mission choices; forced sales import that constraint.
insights.quote: The corporate form in which Craigslist operates, however, is not an appropriate vehicle for purely philanthropic ends, at least not when there are other stockholders

insights.claim: Per the author's reading of eBay v. Newmark, once a single outside investor exists, controlling owners cannot justify decisions by their own conception of company purpose alone and must operate within fiduciary obligations.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Minority stakes acquired from forced sellers can carry outsized leverage over controlling founders.
insights.quote: Once there is a single outside investor, the controlling shareholders must exercise their authority within the constraints of fiduciary obligations
insights.locator: The ruling of eBay v. Newmark

insights.claim: eBay acquired its Craigslist minority stake from a former third shareholder exiting, then launched a competitor, illustrating how a single minority sale can introduce an adversarial owner.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Secondary sales of founder-company stakes can be a strategic entry point for competitors.
insights.locator: At the time, Jim and Craig

themes.theme: Takings Clause challenge to wealth taxes

insights.claim: The author argues that between ordinary taxes and confiscation there must be a constitutional boundary, since a 100% 'tax' on asset value is functionally a taking without compensation.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Wealth taxes face credible constitutional litigation risk that could delay or void collection.
insights.quote: Somewhere, then, between ordinary taxes and confiscation, there must be some constitutionally protected boundary.

insights.claim: A hypothetical wartime 'property tax' equal to 100% of a farmer's tungsten-inflated land value would force sale of the land, achieving the same result as condemnation without the compensation the Takings Clause requires.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Illustrates how taxes on illiquid appreciated assets can force sales even when income does not support the liability.

insights.claim: Supreme Court precedent already protects personal property, intangible business assets, going-concern value, and contractual rights under the Takings Clause, so courts will have to decide whether control itself is protected.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
entities: Kimball Laundry Co. v. United States
Louisville Joint Stock Land Bank v. Radford
insights.so_what: A ruling that control rights are protected property would sharply limit wealth-tax design nationwide.
insights.quote: The wealth tax will force the courts to consider if control itself is protected.

insights.claim: The author concedes the tax/taking line is extraordinarily hard to draw, because almost any tax can require asset sales and declaring such taxes unconstitutional would make most taxation impossible.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Constitutional challenges are not a sure thing; investors should not assume courts will block Prop 40.
insights.quote: Drawing that boundary is extraordinarily difficult.

themes.theme: Private companies as infrastructure of liberty

insights.claim: Private companies convert constitutional rights like speech and association into material capacity to act, so forcing them into diffuse ownership erodes private agency beyond revenue effects.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Frames wealth-tax opposition as a liberty issue, broadening the political coalition against such measures.
insights.quote: In the modern world, private companies are how our constitutional rights are exercised in practice.

insights.claim: The constitutional question extends beyond California's billionaires to whether the state can force Americans to surrender the institutions through which they exercise independence, especially at lower federal thresholds.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Family businesses and mid-size founders, not just billionaires, are the long-run exposure if federal versions advance.
